Listen to this article Share Most investing lessons tell you what to buy. This one is about what to avoid. In The Money, people lose to bad decisions, which often outweigh the money they make from good ones. Avoiding a big loss is worth more than chasing a big gain, because a loss of 50 per cent needs a gain of 100 per cent just to get you back to where you started. Do not invest in a promise you cannot check. In April 2025, CBEX, an online platform that claimed to trade digital assets, stopped paying withdrawals and shut its offices in Nigeria. Reports put investor losses at about ₦1.3 trillion, spread across roughly 600,000 people. Divide ₦1.3 trillion by 600,000 and you get about ₦2.2 million per investor. For many families, that was years of savings. “Borrowed money has a fixed cost and a due date. Investment returns have neither. If you take a loan at a high interest rate to buy shares or a “sure” scheme, the lender gets paid whether you win or lose. When the investment falls, you still owe the full loan, plus interest.” CBEX offered 100 percent returns in 30 days. Do the arithmetic on that promise. If ₦500,000 doubles every month for a year, it becomes ₦500,000 multiplied by 2 twelve times, or about ₦2.05 billion. No legitimate investment compounds money like that. A return that cannot exist is the first sign of a scheme that pays old members with new members’ money. The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) of Nigeria said afterwards that CBEX was never registered to operate in the Nigerian capital market. Its Director General went further and said the Commission could do nothing to help victims recover the money. Keep that in mind. When an unregistered platform fails, there is often nobody to call. Check the licence before you check the return. The SEC keeps a portal of registered capital market operators at sec.gov.ng/cmos. Before you send money to any fund manager, broker or investment app, search for the company there. It takes five minutes. If the name is not on the list, stop. Do not accept a screenshot of a certificate as proof. Search the portal yourself. A licence does not mean the investment will make money. It means a regulator supervises the firm, and there is a process when things go wrong. Under the Investments and Securities Act 2025, promoters of Ponzi schemes now face a fine of at least ₦20 million, up to 10 years in prison, or both. That law protects you only if you deal with something the law can see. Do not let a friend’s profit become your plan Ponzi schemes spread through many channels, including WhatsApp groups and family networks. The early members really do get paid, and they tell you so with screenshots. That is how the scheme grows. Your cousin’s withdrawal last month tells you nothing about whether yours will clear next month. Ask two questions of any investment a friend brings. Where does the return come from? Who holds my money? If the answer to the first is “trading” with no detail, and the answer to the second is “the platform”, walk away. Do not buy what you do not understand. A simple test helps. If you cannot explain to your spouse in two sentences how the investment makes money, you are not ready to own it. A Treasury bill earns because the federal government borrows from you and pays interest. A share in a listed bank earns because the bank lends, collects fees and pays dividends from its profit. You can read the bank’s accounts. Those are investments you can explain. A token that pays 5 per cent a week because of “arbitrage” is not. Do not put everything in one place. Even good investments disappoint. A listed company can have a bad year, and a property can sit empty for months. If all your savings sit in one asset, one bad outcome becomes your whole outcome. Spread your money across a few things you understand. Keep the cash you need within a year in safe, short instruments. Put long-term money in a mix of shares and bonds through funds if you do not have time to pick them yourself. Your Retirement Savings Account is already part of that mix, so count it. Do not borrow to invest. Borrowed money has a fixed cost and a due date. Investment returns have neither. If you take a loan at a high interest rate to buy shares or a “sure” scheme, the lender gets paid whether you win or lose. When the investment falls, you still owe the full loan, plus interest. The same applies to selling your car, emptying your RSA where the rules allow, or taking money meant for rent or school fees. Invest only money you can leave alone through a bad year. Do not chase what has already moved. When a stock or a coin has doubled, everyone hears about it. That is usually the most expensive time to buy. The price already reflects the good news, and late buyers often provide the exit for early ones. Price is not value. Before you buy a share, look at what the company earns and what you are paying for those earnings. If you cannot find the earnings, you are buying a story. In closing Good investing is also defensive. Check the licence on the SEC portal. Do the arithmetic on every promised return. Know where your money sits and who supervises it. Keep borrowed money and next term’s school fees out of it. The return you are promised is a claim. The licence, the custodian and the accounts are the evidence. Ask for the evidence first. Education only. Kalu A. Aja is a Certified Financial Education Instructor and an astute professional with over 27 years of experience spanning capital market operations, treasury, investment, asset management, and occupational pension services.
